changes: Make the card state explicitly that custodial responsibility extends to future generations, since the brief names this and the card only implies it through knowledge being passed on.

Change the question b scenario from a New South Wales fire agency and forest to a Victorian setting, such as a Victorian land manager working with Traditional Owners, so the example is local to the Victorian course.
match.reason: The bank point teaches the same idea at the right depth, but it needs a small addition about future generations and a Victorian example to suit this course.

confirm.reason: The closest bank point, Care for Country, is broader: it also covers what Country means, cultural burning and modern land and fire management, and it never states the idea of caring for Country on behalf of future generations, so a narrower card on custodial responsibility is needed.

rejected.title: Custodial responsibility
card: For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, Country means land, waters, sky and all living things, and the connections between them. People are part of Country, not separate from it.
Because of this connection, people have a duty to look after Country. This is called custodial responsibility.
The duty is to care for Country so that future generations can live with it and learn from it. It is a duty passed down, not a right to own or use up.
This care is guided by knowledge built up over tens of thousands of years and handed on through stories, practice and Elders.
rejected.remember: Caring for Country is a duty to look after it for those who come after.

a.q: What does custodial responsibility mean for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples?
opts: A duty to care for Country for future generations
A right to own and sell parts of Country
A duty to keep people out of Country
A right to use Country as much as needed
a.why: Custodial responsibility is a duty to look after Country so that later generations can live with it. The option about using Country as much as needed is tempting, but the card says the duty is not a right to use it up.
a.clue: Think of a duty passed down, not a right to take.

b.q: An Elder teaches young people on the coast how to read the seasons and look after the shoreline. Which idea does this best show?
opts: Knowledge is handed on so Country is cared for
Knowledge is kept private so Country is protected
Country is cared for only when it is in use
Country is cared for by those who own it
b.why: The Elder is passing on knowledge built over a very long time so the next generation can care for Country. Ownership is tempting, but custodial responsibility is a duty of care, not a claim of ownership.
b.clue: Who is the knowledge being passed to, and why?

version.title: Custodial responsibility
card: For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, Country is the land, waters and sky of a group, with its plants, animals, stories and law. People are part of Country.
Custodial responsibility is the duty to care for Country. It is passed down from Elders and ancestors, and handed on in turn to children.
The care looks ahead. People use Country for food and materials, but they take what they need so it stays healthy for the generations to come.
This care is guided by knowledge of seasons, plants, animals and water, built over tens of thousands of years and shared through stories, songs, ceremony and practice.
version.remember: Caring for Country is a duty handed down, so it stays healthy for those who come next.

a.q: Which statement best describes custodial responsibility?
opts: A duty to care for Country so it stays healthy in future
A duty to keep Country untouched and never use it at all
A set of rules that governments write for land managers
A freedom for each person to use Country as they choose
a.why: Custodial responsibility is a duty, passed down, to care for Country for the generations to come. Keeping Country untouched is tempting, but people do use Country for food and materials, taking what they need.
a.clue: Think about who the care is for.

b.q: On a stretch of coast, Elders teach young people to leave the shellfish beds alone at certain times of year, so there will be plenty in years to come. Which idea does this show?
opts: Looking after Country for the generations ahead
Keeping Country unchanged by never using it
Saving food now so it can be traded later on
Following the rules set out in a fishing licence
b.why: The Elders pass on knowledge so the shellfish stay plentiful for those who come later, which is caring for Country for future generations. The beds are only left at certain times, so this is not about never using Country.
b.clue: Who will benefit from the shellfish being left alone?

a.best: A duty to care for Country so it stays healthy in future

b.best: Looking after Country for the generations ahead
